terms.comment: Masculine; feminine in the singular for a fixed or appointed day (diē cōnstitūtā: Caes. BG 1.4.2, Lewis & Short), and often in verse. Also the daylight hours, as against the night: by day is interdiū (see by day).

evidence: Cic. Att. 5.1.3: haec ego patior cotīdiē
terms.comment: Lewis & Short prints cottīdiē, with cotīdiē beside it; the house writes cotīdiē, as in the lexicon’s name.

evidence: Caes. BG 1.1.4: quod ferē cotīdiānīs proeliīs cum Germānīs contendunt
Cic. Fam. 9.21.1: epistulās vērō cotīdiānīs verbīs texere solēmus
terms.comment: The adjective of cotīdiē: what happens every day, and so what is usual or ordinary. Lewis & Short prints cottīdiānus; the house spelling follows cotīdiē.

evidence: Plaut. Persa 115: id tōtum prōcēdit diem

phrases.latin: ēn, inquit, mihi haec ego patior cotīdiē
phrases.english: ‘You see?’ he said to me. ‘This is what I put up with every day.’
but you are dawdling, and the day is slipping away

phrases.latin: ex eā diē ad hanc diem
